title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 39
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: A Bed Among Strangers
passages.text:
A. Paying to sleep in a building owned by someone you do not know is a stranger arrangement than its familiarity suggests. It requires a traveller to trust an unknown host with their person and belongings while asleep, and a host to admit an unknown traveller to their premises, and for most of history the arrangement was managed not by contract but by the innkeeper's liability, which was unusually strict: an innkeeper was answerable for a guest's goods in a way ordinary tradesmen were not.

B. Early inns were shaped by the animals rather than the people. A traveller arrived on horseback or by coach, and the establishment's essential facilities were stabling, fodder and a yard large enough to turn a vehicle; the accommodation for humans was secondary, often a shared room and sometimes a shared bed. What looks like indifference to comfort was a correct allocation of space to the expensive and perishable part of the journey.

C. The railway destroyed the coaching inn and created the hotel. Travellers no longer arrived in small groups at intervals along a road but in large numbers at a fixed point at a fixed time, which made a much larger building viable and located it beside the station. The private bedroom, the dining room open to non-residents and the public lounge all follow from that change in arrival pattern.

D. Standardisation arrived with the traveller who could not inspect in advance. Once a person might book from another city or country, the value of knowing what would be provided exceeded the value of local character, and chains grew by offering a room whose contents were predictable. The much-criticised sameness of such rooms is the product they are selling rather than a failure of imagination.

E. The economics turn on a fact the industry rarely states plainly. A hotel's costs are almost entirely fixed — the building, its finance, and a minimum staff — while an unsold room earns nothing and cannot be stored, so the last rooms of any night are worth whatever anyone will pay. This is why prices for the same room vary by a factor of several within a week and why the industry adopted algorithmic pricing earlier than most.

F. What short-term letting platforms changed is less about competition than about who bears the costs. Supply expanded by using housing stock as accommodation, which met demand and removed dwellings in cities where they were scarce; the effects on rents are contested in magnitude and consistent in direction. The regulatory difficulty is that the same activity is a household earning a little from a spare room and a business operating an unlicensed hotel, and no simple rule separates them.

passages.title: Reading the Rings
passages.text:
A tree records its own history in a form that can be read with a hand lens. In climates with a distinct growing season, each year's growth appears as a ring, wide in a favourable year and narrow in a poor one, and the sequence of widths in a single trunk is a record of the conditions that tree experienced. The method that grew out of this observation is more powerful than the simple picture suggests, and its power comes from matching rather than from counting.

The matching is the essential technique. The pattern of wide and narrow rings over several decades is effectively a signature shared by trees in a region, so a sequence from a living tree can be overlapped with one from an older timber whose rings end where the living record begins, and that timber with an older one again. Chained in this way, records extend thousands of years beyond any living tree, and a piece of wood of unknown age can be placed in that chain by finding where its pattern fits.

The dating this produces is exact in a way most archaeological methods are not. A matched sequence gives a calendar year, not a range with an error term, and where bark remains it gives the season of felling. This is why dendrochronology became the calibration standard against which other dating methods were checked, rather than merely another method alongside them.

The climate information is real and narrower than often assumed. A ring width responds to whatever limited growth in that place: in a dry region, rainfall; near the cold limit of a species, summer temperature; in a wet temperate wood, possibly neither in any legible way. Reconstructions therefore work well where a single factor dominates and poorly where several interact, which is why the most useful sequences come from trees growing in difficult places rather than comfortable ones.

Several complications are routinely underestimated. Trees can produce two rings in a year of unusual weather or none at all in a very poor one, so counting alone is unreliable and only cross-matching between many trees resolves it; a tree's rings also narrow as it ages for reasons of geometry rather than climate, and that trend must be removed before any climate signal can be read. Both problems are handled and neither is trivial.

The most valuable application may be the least expected. Because timber in old buildings can be dated to the year, the construction history of standing structures can be established without documents, and rebuilding, repair and extension can be distinguished and sequenced. Buildings whose recorded history was thought settled have been substantially redated, generally in the direction of being more altered and less original than assumed.

passages.title: The Car That Comes When Called
passages.text:
The taxi problem is a matching problem, and the reason it resisted solution for a century is that neither party could see the other. A person wanting a ride and a driver wanting a fare were often a short distance apart with no way to know it, so drivers cruised empty and passengers waited, and the waste was borne by both. Dispatch by telephone improved this and required an operator to hold in mind what a map now holds automatically.

Regulation of the old industry addressed real problems and produced predictable side effects. Limiting the number of vehicles was intended to prevent congestion and ensure drivers could earn a living, and where the limit was transferable it became an asset whose price reflected the value of the restriction — sometimes exceeding the price of a house. The rents created by that scarcity accrued to whoever held the permit rather than to the driver, who frequently rented it.

What the platforms supplied first was information rather than cars. Showing each party where the other was, settling payment without cash, and recording both sides' conduct removed the frictions that had made the market work badly, and the improvement in service was immediate and genuine. Much of the argument since has confused this contribution, which is real, with the labour arrangements and pricing practices that accompanied it, which are separate questions.

The pricing that varies with demand is the practice most disliked and most defensible. When more people want rides than there are drivers, a higher price both allocates the available cars to those who most need them and draws more drivers onto the road, and suppressing it produces a shortage instead of a price rise — a queue rather than a bill. The objection that it charges most when need is greatest is not answered by this, and remains the strongest thing said against it.

Whether drivers gained is the question with the least settled answer. Earnings per hour are contested and depend heavily on how unpaid waiting time and vehicle costs are counted; flexibility of hours is genuinely valued and is not usually available in employment; and the classification of drivers as contractors rather than employees transfers risks — of illness, of vehicle depreciation, of a slow week — onto the person least able to absorb them. Different jurisdictions have answered this differently and none has answered it well.

The congestion outcome is the finding that most contradicted expectation. Cities where these services grew have generally seen more vehicle traffic rather than less, because trips that would have been made by public transport, on foot or not at all are now made by car, and because vehicles travel empty between fares. A service that reduces the need to own a car has increased the number of cars moving, which is a reminder that convenience and efficiency are not the same measurement.
